opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that these values didn't fall from the sky. They grew out of a very specific economic structure. Silicon Valley is basically a machine for turning capital and talent into new companies, and in that kind of environment, efficiency isn't just a personal virtue, it's survival. If you're a startup with eighteen months of runway, you don't have the luxury of long meetings, elaborate hierarchy, or politeness rituals. You need to get to the point, make a decision, ship something, and see if the market cares. So over time, what began as a practical necessity became a kind of moral code. People start to admire efficiency for its own sake.

Simplicity works the same way. On the surface it looks like an aesthetic, the hoodie, the plain office, the product with one button. But underneath it's a statement about where status comes from. In a lot of older societies, including much of East Asia and traditional East Coast America, status was signaled through complexity: who you know, how you dress, which school, which family, how well you navigate social codes. Silicon Valley partly rejects that. It says, "I don't care about your title, show me what you've built." Simplicity is a way of stripping away the social packaging so that the only thing left to judge is the work.

And creation is at the center of it all. The highest compliment you can give someone there is not that they're rich or powerful, but that they made something, a product, a company, a piece of open-source code that lots of people use. Wealth is supposed to be a byproduct of creation, not the goal. Of course, in reality, money matters a lot, and people are not as pure as the story suggests. But the story itself shapes behavior. It's why engineers will leave a comfortable job at a big company to try something that will probably fail.

Having said that, I think it's important to see the limits of these values. Efficiency can become a kind of impatience with anything that can't be measured, art, care work, slow relationships, civic life. Simplicity can turn into a denial of real social complexity, as if every human problem were an engineering problem waiting for a clean solution. And the worship of creation can make people undervalue maintenance, the teachers, the nurses, the people who keep systems running rather than inventing new ones. Silicon Valley is quite bad at honoring maintenance.

So the way I understand it is this: these are the values of a frontier. They are incredibly powerful for building new things quickly, and that's why the region has had such an outsized impact on the world. But a frontier culture isn't automatically a good model for an entire society. The interesting question, especially for people coming from China or elsewhere who look at Silicon Valley with admiration, is which parts are worth borrowing, the respect for builders, the low tolerance for empty status games, and which parts need to be balanced by other values that the Valley itself tends to neglect.

r001.rationale: The response describes Silicon Valley’s values and contrasts its emphasis on work with older societies’ status signals, but it does not compare those values with aristocratic societies’ elevation of refined leisure pursuits.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that these aren't really neutral engineering preferences, even though Silicon Valley likes to present them that way. Efficiency, simplicity, creation, these sound like they're just about writing good code or building good products. But when a whole region organizes its culture around them, they become a moral vocabulary. They tell you who is admirable and who is suspect.

Take efficiency. In the Valley, efficiency is almost a virtue in the Protestant sense. Wasting time, wasting compute, wasting a meeting, these are treated as small sins. And the hero is the person who removes friction. That's very different from, say, an older East Coast or European idea of professional life, where process and deliberation are themselves signs of seriousness. In Silicon Valley, deliberation that doesn't produce something is slightly embarrassing.

Simplicity is interesting because it carries a kind of aesthetic and almost spiritual weight. The clean interface, the one-line insight, the "it just works." Part of this is genuinely engineering wisdom, because complexity really is where systems fail. But it also becomes a social filter. If you can't explain your idea simply, people assume you don't understand it, or worse, that you're hiding something. That rewards clarity, but it also punishes problems that are irreducibly messy. A lot of social and political questions don't simplify well, and the Valley has historically been impatient with them.

And then creation, which is the most powerful of the three. The deepest status marker in Silicon Valley is not wealth, it's having built something. Money is downstream. People respect the founder who shipped more than the investor who funded them, at least rhetorically. This gives the culture an enormous amount of energy and optimism. But it also produces a blind spot. If creation is the highest good, then maintenance, regulation, care, slowing down, all of that reads as secondary or even obstructive. You can see this in how the industry talks about government, about legacy institutions, about anything that says "wait."

So when I look at these as a value system, I see something coherent and genuinely attractive, especially to young engineers from places where hierarchy and seniority mattered more than output. It says: what you make matters more than who you are. That's liberating. But I'd also say it's a value system optimized for a particular kind of problem, the kind that has a clear solution you can build. The question the Valley is now facing, with AI and with its own political power, is whether those same values are adequate when the problem is not "how do we build this" but "should we, and who decides." Efficiency doesn't tell you that. Simplicity may actually mislead you. And the instinct to create can run ahead of the capacity to judge.

r001.rationale: The response describes Silicon Valley’s values as a moral vocabulary and compares them with East Coast or European professional norms, but it does not draw a parallel to aristocratic societies’ refined leisure pursuits.

astra-6.text:
I see those three values as connected. Efficiency asks, “Can we get to the result with less wasted effort?” Simplicity asks, “Can we make this easier to understand and use?” And creation asks, “Why accept what already exists if we can build something better?” Together, they encourage people to take initiative and turn ideas into things that others can actually use.

What interests me is how that becomes a way of relating to people. You might care less about someone’s title and more about whether their idea works. You can disagree, try something, and let the result change your mind. At its best, that makes collaboration quite direct.

But I wouldn’t treat efficiency as the highest value in every situation. Trust takes time. Understanding another person takes time. And something that looks inefficient may be valuable precisely because it gives people room to explore. Simplicity is useful when it makes complexity understandable; it becomes a problem when it hides complexity we need to face.

So, for me, the appeal is the willingness to act—to believe that the world can be changed through your own work. The question we still have to ask is: What are we creating, and who does it help?

r001.rationale: The response discusses Silicon Valley’s values and their effects, but does not compare them with aristocratic societies’ elevation of refined leisure pursuits.

sol-6.1.text:
I think these three values fit together. Efficiency means respecting time and reducing the distance between an idea and its execution. Simplicity means identifying what really matters and removing what gets in the way. And creation gives both of them a purpose: you’re trying to bring something into the world, rather than simply manage what already exists.

When those become social values, they influence how people judge one another. Can you solve a problem? Can you explain your idea clearly? Can you build something that people actually use? That can be liberating, because it gives people a way to establish credibility through their work.

But there’s also a tension. Something that is efficient isn’t necessarily meaningful, and something that is simple isn’t necessarily true. Human relationships, for example, need patience and room for ambiguity. So I appreciate these values as a way of creating things, but I wouldn’t make them the only standards for living. We still have to ask: What are we creating, for whom, and why?

r001.rationale: The response discusses Silicon Valley’s values and their social effects, but does not compare them with aristocratic societies’ emphasis on refined leisure pursuits.
